# Execution Harnesses and Tool Isolation {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."
>
> — John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan" [@Culkin1967Schoolman, p. 70]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What is an architecture design environment, and what must it provide for AI-native work?*

**Core thesis:** *An environment is not a simulator wrapper; it coordinates state, tools, workloads, interfaces, failure handling, and multi-fidelity execution to enable closed-loop automated design.*
:::

A tool command is not an environment. An architect can launch a simulator, compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow and still be unable to say which candidate ran, which state the tool inherited, what an unfamiliar warning meant, or whether a retry repeated the same work. Generative models and automated optimizers widen that gap, because they can propose candidates far faster than tools can evaluate them, and every proposal becomes a run that shares licenses, scratch storage, and compute with the others.

On a shared cluster, tool state can be corrupted, license servers can run out of available checkouts, intermediate checkpoints can fill scratch storage, and a generated Tcl script can attempt arbitrary system calls. An execution environment contains each run and binds every returned metric to the recorded inputs, tool versions, and operating conditions that produced it.

Wrappers, harnesses, and isolated sandboxes assemble that environment (@fig-ch06-cover-map). Setup defines the fixed inputs, typed interfaces, and artifact lineage before a study begins, while runtime manages concurrent job dispatch, license contention, checkpoint recovery, and error containment once jobs are running. The prospective Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR) system-on-chip (SoC) study illustrates these responsibilities across several tool interfaces: its analytical static random-access memory (SRAM) screen runs through an actual model, whereas its downstream simulation and physical-implementation steps remain unexecuted. Here the focus is on how the environment runs tools safely and records what executed, what failed, and what returned; @sec-feedback-verification-trust then examines how to judge whether those returned observations are trustworthy enough to steer the design.

![**Nested boundaries turn authorized requests into qualified execution records.** The environment separates tool wrappers, execution harnesses, and outer sandboxes so that each run isolates tool state, records compute and license costs, and logs the metadata needed to audit simulation and synthesis outputs before they drive the next design step. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/ch06-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch06-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which nested environment, harness, wrapper, and tool boundaries turn an authorized request into a complete execution record for later qualification."}

## Architecture of the Tool Execution Harness

Consider an automated optimizer searching the cache hierarchy candidates introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. When the optimizer requests an evaluation of one candidate under a target memory workload, the environment validates the typed request, maps the parameter vector to simulator configuration files, sets CPU affinity and memory limits on a compute node, and launches the simulator binary. After the process exits, the harness parses the log files, extracts miss rates and cycle counts, records the consumed core-hours and memory footprint, and returns a structured execution record that the optimizer can inspect to choose its next candidate.

Now consider what happens when a twelve-hour full-system simulation fails at hour eight from an out-of-memory kernel kill and a naive script immediately relaunches the command. Before trusting the new result, the architect has to answer three operational questions: did the restart resume from a clean memory checkpoint or start over from cold reset, did it inherit modified host environment variables or leftover scratch files from the failed attempt, and did the accounting log charge the lost eight core-hours against the study's compute budget? Because a bare shell retry discards that failure context, later comparisons can silently mix a cold start with a resumed run or undercount the true cost of the search.

An execution environment therefore provides both an external interface for the exploration method and the operational machinery behind that interface: whereas the external interface defines what actions a method can request and what structured feedback returns, the internal machinery orchestrates the processes, isolated filesystems, license tokens, and hardware resources required to carry out those actions safely. In an interactive computer-aided design (CAD) flow, human engineers handle this housekeeping by hand, inspecting logs, cleaning scratch directories, and watching license queues; an automated loop has to do the same work in software across dozens of concurrent candidates and heterogeneous tools.[^fn-sandboxing-kubernetes-c06] Separating the layers that perform this work lets a team start with a minimal harness and expand it as the study grows.

[^fn-sandboxing-kubernetes-c06]: **The orchestration parallel**: A correct tool script does not by itself control the state of concurrent or interrupted runs. Containers and workflow schedulers provide useful mechanisms for software execution, but an architecture environment must also coordinate tool-specific checkpoints, shared CAD licenses, and restricted design inputs. The harness performs this coordination for generated requests as well as requests written by an engineer.


### From Tools to an Execution Environment

Suppose a generative model proposes a revised cache coherence controller in register-transfer level (RTL) code and a team evaluates it with a single monolithic shell script that writes the testbench driver, runs Verilator, searches the terminal log with regular expressions, and immediately launches gate-level synthesis in Yosys. The first time two candidates run at once or a simulator upgrade alters a warning message, that script breaks: concurrent runs overwrite the same scratch files, a log-parsing failure looks identical to an RTL assertion error, and synthesis launches on a candidate that never passed its functional check. Inside the environment boundary, separating five distinct layers prevents those responsibilities from collapsing into one brittle script:

- **Tool**: The standalone executable that performs a domain-specific transformation or analysis, such as compiling software with LLVM, synthesizing RTL code into gates with Yosys, or evaluating physical timing with OpenSTA. It consumes files in proprietary or standard formats and emits log reports or physical artifacts.
- **Simulator**: A specialized class of tool that models hardware or software behavior over time. For example, gem5 executes an event-driven, cycle-level microarchitectural model, yielding cycle counts, cache hit distributions, and bus contention statistics under configured workload assumptions.
- **Wrapper**: The adapter that bridges an individual tool to the environment's typed contract. It validates request parameters, generates tool-specific command scripts and configuration files, manages process invocation, parses unstructured text logs into strongly typed metrics, and flags syntax or runtime errors.
- **Harness**: The workflow coordinator that orchestrates multi-tool execution pipelines. It resolves candidate dependency graphs, manages concurrent dispatch, arbitrates shared resources such as license tokens and GPU queues, handles timeouts and retries, and binds execution outcomes to parent artifacts.
- **Environment**: The overarching system that encapsulates the design state, permitted action space, tool interfaces, and security sandboxes. It governs what the search method can observe, modify, and evaluate, establishing the boundary between the search method and tool execution.

On that coherence-controller check, each layer handles a separate piece of the job. The wrapper generates the testbench driver, launches Verilator inside an isolated scratch directory, and extracts assertion outcomes. The harness tracks the run, logs its memory and CPU consumption, and triggers downstream gate-level synthesis through Yosys only after the functional check passes. Surrounding both, the environment dictates whether the generator may modify arbitrary state machines, tune clock periods in a Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file, or merely sweep buffer capacities within a fixed netlist. Supporting generated microarchitectures therefore means handling new code artifacts and changing dependency graphs, rather than merely sweeping scalar parameters across a static model.

How much of this machinery a study needs depends on which of the three operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers it targets (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration). For Layer 1 work, execution usually remains open-loop: a generative model proposes an isolated code snippet, such as a first-in, first-out (FIFO) buffer or an arbiter, and the human engineer acts as the execution harness by pasting generated RTL into a local workspace, invoking the compiler or simulator through interactive shell scripts, and inspecting terminal logs to diagnose syntax errors or port mismatches.

For Layer 2 work, the environment must support automated parameter search within a frozen structural container $\Theta$. As an optimizer sweeps architectural parameters $\theta$, such as cache capacities, queue depths, or macro floorplan coordinates, the environment dispatches runs across simulators and estimators such as gem5, Ramulator 2, and analytical models to evaluate many variations. Because the hardware template and external interfaces stay fixed, these faster evaluations can guide the search once the study has checked them against more detailed analysis over the parameter range in use; that calibration is an obligation of the study, not a property the container supplies on its own.

Layer 3 work permits coordinated changes beyond that template, so candidates can step outside the range where a fast estimator was calibrated. While early checks can still filter out broken proposals, candidates that advance toward implementation must pass through physical design and signoff tools inside the environment rather than a single simulator; a public system reporting such an end-to-end run from a written specification to a timing-closed layout is examined against the book's evidence standard in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect.

To assemble such a multi-tool flow without building every adapter from scratch, a team can build on existing electronic design automation (EDA) frameworks: SiliconCompiler connects design data, tool settings, and process design kit (PDK) information through a shared schema and execution flow [@SiliconCompiler], whereas Hammer separates tool-specific steps, technology information, and project configuration behind plugin interfaces [@Hammer]. These frameworks handle the mechanics of invoking hardware tools, but the study still has to define which actions its methods can request, how returned results re-enter the design loop, and how shared cluster resources are protected when many evaluations run concurrently.

### Host and Network Boundaries

Every evaluation request runs on a host with finite compute, shared storage, and access to project data. When an automated loop dispatches many runs in parallel, they compete for licenses, processors, and storage bandwidth, while any generated script can affect whatever files or network connections its process can reach. Controlling both resource sharing and host access requires attention to five practical boundaries, whose exact mechanisms depend on the tools, cluster deployment, and study restrictions:

1. **Shared licenses.** Commercial EDA tools often require a license checkout managed by servers such as FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] or Sentinel before work can proceed. Adding compute workers cannot increase throughput once seats are exhausted, and an unconstrained loop can starve other engineers on the cluster. The harness therefore tracks each request's license requirements alongside its CPU and memory requirements, queues work when capacity is unavailable, and monitors checkout status. While a local token pool can coordinate the harness's own requests, it cannot reserve capacity against external users, and recovery after a worker failure must follow the license server's timeout and reclamation policy rather than assuming a terminated process has immediately freed its seat.

2. **Restricted data.** Many studies allow an external model to propose design changes while requiring foundry models and proprietary design files to remain on approved internal hosts. The environment must enforce those restrictions for process design kit (PDK) collateral, layout views, transistor-level models, and any derived information covered by the study's disclosure policy. Putting a proxy between an external model and internal tools is only part of the job, because the return path needs equal attention: replacing absolute delays with "Path A is 12% slower than Path B" or stripping die coordinates from a congestion map reduces detail without proving that the output may be disclosed, and prompts or abstract syntax tree (AST) edits can also carry proprietary circuit structure. The environment therefore needs an explicit policy defining what may cross this boundary, including feedback from synthesis, design rule checking (DRC), and layout versus schematic (LVS) checks.

3. **Host runtime variation.** A simulator's elapsed wall-clock time reflects the host machine as well as the modeled design, because worker migration across non-uniform memory access (NUMA)[^fn-numa-c06] nodes, competing memory traffic, and central processing unit (CPU) frequency scaling all alter execution speed. Where runtime comparisons matter, controlled resource allocation keeps those measurements interpretable: on Linux, CPU affinity tools such as `taskset -c` restrict where threads run while scheduler rules prevent unwanted contention on those cores, CPU frequency policies and storage placement can be pinned, and RAM-backed temporary storage (`/dev/shm` or `tmpfs`) absorbs I/O when its memory footprint fits the allocation. Although these controls reduce host interference, they do not make a nondeterministic tool deterministic; @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion separates host timing variation from changes in returned design results.

4. **Generated scripts and host access.** Synthesis and layout scripts are executable programs: Tcl commands such as `exec` and pipeline forms of `open` can launch arbitrary shell commands with the permissions of the tool process, allowing a generated script to overwrite files or make network requests beyond the intended design operation. To grant a run only the files, permissions, and network access it requires, an environment can combine unprivileged Open Container Initiative (OCI) containers, user namespaces, read-only library and PDK mounts, restricted network interfaces, and kernel system-call filters such as seccomp.[^fn-seccomp-c06] Each mechanism addresses a different facet of isolation, so a container alone does not establish a safe boundary if exposed bind mounts and file permissions remain overly broad.

5. **Storage and retained artifacts.** Physical design tools write multi-gigabyte databases, checkpoints, and exchange files, including Synopsys NDM databases, Design Exchange Format (DEF) layout data, Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) parasitics, and GDSII mask streams,[^fn-physical-checkpoints-c06] so concurrent writes can saturate shared network storage and leave processors waiting on disk I/O. Writing active runs to node-local scratch storage avoids that bottleneck, provided the harness moves needed outputs to persistent storage before reclaiming the workspace. What must be kept depends on subsequent work: a parser failure requires the raw text reports, an interrupted run needs its checkpoint to resume, and human review often requires more than extracted summary metrics. Failed or filtered candidates still need the files required for recovery and audit, whereas bulky intermediate databases can be deleted once those uses finish so long as the retained execution record states what remains available.

[^fn-flexlm-c06]: **License checkout**: A tool requests access to a licensed feature before using it. Depending on the tool's integration with the license manager, unavailable capacity may cause the request to wait or fail; the harness must distinguish that outcome from an analysis that ran and found a design problem.

[^fn-numa-c06]: **NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access)**: A computer memory design where memory access time depends on the memory location relative to the processor. Under NUMA, a processor can access its own local memory faster than non-local memory (memory local to another processor or shared between processors).

[^fn-seccomp-c06]: **seccomp (secure computing mode)**: A Linux kernel feature that restricts the system calls a process can make, reducing the exposed kernel surface. It is one component of containment, not a complete sandbox.

[^fn-physical-checkpoints-c06]: **Physical design checkpoints**: During chip layout, tools generate massive intermediate files. DEF (Design Exchange Format) stores the placement and routing of components. SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format) records the resistance and capacitance of the wires for timing analysis. GDSII is the final binary format representing the 2D shapes of the chip's masks, ultimately sent to the foundry for manufacturing.


### Tool Wrappers

Once host and network controls bound where a tool can run and what files it can touch, a tool wrapper connects the search method's typed request to the executable running inside those limits. Suppose a generator submits revised controller RTL for synthesis under a specified clock constraint and cell library. If the tool falls back to a default clock period or loads a different library view, it answers the wrong architectural question even if it exits cleanly. The wrapper must therefore translate the request explicitly, report any mismatch it can detect, and refuse the request whenever the backend tool's interface cannot express a required setting.

Before launching the tool, the wrapper checks that the request contains all required fields, resolves artifact identifiers to the intended source files and libraries on disk, verifies that numeric parameters lie within their allowed ranges, and writes auxiliary files such as the controller's SDC clock definition. Catching malformed inputs before launch saves cluster compute and commercial license tokens, though passing these pre-flight checks only confirms that the request is well formed, not that the hardware design is correct or that the tool run will succeed.

The return path needs the same care: once execution yields a process exit code alongside log reports and physical artifacts, a dedicated parser extracts typed metrics, units, and operating conditions while retaining the raw logs for auditability. The harness then binds these outputs to the originating request and records consumed compute and license resources, because keeping these steps separate prevents a translation error or an unparseable log from masquerading as a design result (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**Tool wrappers separate raw execution state from semantic result interpretation.** The wrapper validates and translates incoming typed requests before invoking backend tools, while the parser extracts structured attributes and retains unclassified residual output. The harness binds runtime outcomes, parse health, compute costs, and lineage into an immutable execution record. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-environment-tool-interface.svg){#fig-environment-tool-interface width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which an architecture question and workload, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter the tool-connected environment as a typed request. The wrapper validates and translates the request before calling the tool. An invalid request goes directly to the harness record. The tool separately produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome that can be failed, partial, or complete. The parser turns retained raw material into structured attributes, unclassified residual output, and a parse status. The harness records request and attempt identity, conditions, runtime outcome, artifacts, parse status, cost, and lineage."}

When an incoming candidate fails pre-flight validation, such as specifying an illegal cache capacity or an unresolvable technology library, the wrapper short-circuits the request directly to the execution record with a refused status, preventing unbudgeted cluster dispatch and preserving license tokens. When execution proceeds, the tool's runtime outcome (failed, partial, or complete) is recorded independently from the parser's extraction status, so downstream methods can distinguish a crashed simulation from a completed run whose report the parser could not read. Whether a wrapper returns a mapped gate-level netlist and static timing slack from synthesis or extracts gem5 miss rates and switching-activity power estimates from simulation, an absent metric always remains distinct from a measured zero. Retaining raw reports alongside unclassified residual output ensures that silent anomalies, such as unconstrained timing paths or missing clock definitions, remain auditable even when a tool exits with code zero.

Separating execution status from log parsing still solves only half the translation problem: a structured return makes tool feedback readable by an algorithm, but a clean exit code and a parsed timing report mean nothing if the tool evaluated the wrong design state. Even when a wrapper formats every command flag and parses every output field properly, the run can still be corrupted if a persistent tool session or scratch directory inherits state from an earlier candidate.

### Managing Stateful Tools and Cross-Stage Translation

A tool's starting state is part of its input, even when that state is absent from the request: a physical-design session may already hold an in-memory netlist, placement, and routing database, or a simulator may resume from a saved checkpoint, as when OpenROAD saves and reloads its design database [@OpenROADDocs]. If a generator submits revised controller RTL while execution resumes from an in-memory database built from the previous candidate, or if a persistent Tcl shell retains stale Design Exchange Format (DEF) floorplan geometries, the resulting report describes the old design under the new candidate's name. Leftover files on a shared `tmpfs` scratch volume cause the same silent corruption when multi-corner static timing analysis (STA) runs read stale Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) extractions or cached timing graphs from an earlier pass.

Launching a fresh process in an empty workspace with a clean environment-variable table is the simplest way to prevent inherited state, provided the wrapper loads the intended inputs and settings. When a study reuses a live session or checkpoint to avoid repeated startup cost, the harness must make that reuse explicit and checkable: a reset must restore the required baseline state, and a deliberate continuation must record the exact checkpoint, in-memory database, and temporary files it builds upon.

State consistency becomes even more demanding when a candidate moves across several tools, because each stage consumes a different representation of the same hardware. Behavioral RTL is synthesized by a tool such as Yosys into a gate-level netlist mapped to a target cell library [@Yosys]. Physical implementation in a flow such as OpenROAD then pairs that netlist with matching library views [@OpenROADDocs]: Liberty (`.lib`) files supply cell timing and power characterization, Library Exchange Format (LEF) files describe physical macro dimensions, pins, and routing blockages, and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF) files specify power domains and isolation rules for a power-aware flow without themselves estimating power.[^fn-eda-formats-c06]

[^fn-eda-formats-c06]: **EDA formats**: Liberty (`.lib`) files describe cell timing and power, while Library Exchange Format (LEF) files describe physical abstractions such as dimensions, pins, and routing obstructions. Unified Power Format (UPF) supplies power intent, including power domains and isolation strategies; it describes requirements for a power-aware implementation rather than supplying that implementation itself.


Merely collecting these files under the same candidate identifier does not guarantee that they still agree. If a generator widens a block's interface while leaving an older LEF physical abstract in place, modifies power domains without updating the UPF power intent, or runs timing analysis against a `.lib` corner characterized at 0.75\ V when the request specifies another supply voltage, the returned timing and power describe a mismatched design or operating condition. The environment must therefore track which inputs each tool path depends on and verify their compatibility before admitting the results.

Translating a request into tool-specific syntax carries a related obligation: a wrapper may convert units or reformat settings, and different tools may legitimately use different abstractions of a candidate when the modeled properties and limitations remain explicit, but silently rounding a buffer capacity or changing an array dimension creates a different candidate. When a backend cannot represent a required feature, the wrapper should report that limitation so the design loop can choose another evaluation path, because changing the candidate just to make a tool run succeed is a new design proposal rather than a translation repair.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Preserve the requested design across every tool boundary"}
**The principle:** A wrapper translates a request into a tool's syntax without changing the candidate, its operating conditions, or its starting state; when it cannot, it refuses the request or reports the limitation.

**The application:** A run that used a default clock, a different library view, a rounded capacity, or state inherited from an earlier attempt still carries the requested candidate's identity while describing a different design. Check translation, starting state, and input compatibility before launch, and give any change made only to get a run through its own identity as a new proposal.
:::

The prospective Lighthouse study illustrates what this translation discipline requires when a single SoC proposal must reach analytical, cycle-level, and RTL tools.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One XR SoC request, several tool representations"}
**Context.** The prospective Lighthouse study illustrates how one candidate can require different tool inputs without changing the design under comparison.

**Application.** Consider a candidate with a 3\ MiB cache, a neural processing unit (NPU) array ($16 \times 16$), and dual LPDDR5X channels. An analytical model would use the dimensions and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) assumptions relevant to its estimates. A configured gem5 model would represent the supported timing behavior, while a Verilator-based path would execute the supplied RTL and testbench. Each path would need matching workload inputs or traffic generators and an explicit account of which candidate features it represents.

**Required behavior.** Wrappers must preserve relevant capacities, dimensions, cache policies, and memory arbitration wherever those properties are modeled. An unsupported feature must be reported rather than silently replaced by a default. Differences between tool outputs must be interpreted in light of their models and conditions. These are requirements for the unexecuted study, not observed wrapper results.
:::

## Pinning Tool Versions, Schemas, and Provenance

If a team launches a multi-day search while passing simulator flags, library corners, and workload binaries through ordinary mutable project directories, a mid-week edit to a shared constraint file or compiler script silently alters the baseline for every subsequent candidate. Enforcing consistent representations across tools therefore starts before the search loop dispatches its first job. During provisioning, the harness freezes shared study inputs and defines how it accepts candidate artifacts (such as revised SystemVerilog modules, simulator configurations, or compiler schedules), how design sources, process libraries, and workload inputs are identified, what typed requests each tool wrapper accepts and returns, and which tool paths evaluate behavioral correctness, cycle-level throughput, or physical timing and power.

The candidates themselves need not all exist when the study begins. As a generator proposes new controller RTL or an optimizer modifies a cache parameter during the loop, the environment registers each new artifact, binds it to the exact library views, constraints, and workload snapshots it requires, and dispatches it to the appropriate tools. Recording those inputs and operating conditions at submission time ensures that every returned report can be traced back to the exact configuration that produced it. The first setup question is therefore how to preserve this lineage as candidate revisions and tool outputs accumulate.

### Lineage and Reproducibility

In a conventional project layout, tools write compiled binaries, elaborated RTL, and synthesized netlists into a single mutable `build/` directory. Once an automated loop branches across dozens of candidates and retries failed runs out of order, in-place builds break down: a late retry overwrites an earlier candidate's synthesis output in place, or a revised RTL module runs timing analysis against a stale netlist from the previous iteration. Knowing which existing artifacts still apply and which must be regenerated requires an explicit dependency graph and recorded *lineage*, the history linking requests, transformations, and artifacts to show which inputs produced an output, which candidate version an evaluation actually used, and how a retry relates to an earlier attempt. To keep that history intact as work proceeds, the environment stores immutable snapshots of source files, constraints, and library views separately from mutable working directories so that later edits never overwrite what an earlier run used.

Compilation and hardware elaboration turn source descriptions into representations that downstream tools can consume, including abstract syntax trees, control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), and gate netlists. A lineage entry connects each output artifact to the exact inputs and settings used to produce it:

- Parent candidate and request identifiers, including the originating attempt when work is retried.
- Transformation tool and compiler versions, together with the settings used.
- Input and output content hashes, which identify the retained file contents.
- Applicable operating conditions and references to the required libraries or models.
- Checks performed on the transformation, their outcomes, and any properties left unchecked.
- Downstream uses permitted by the study, including any restrictions on the resulting artifacts.

Together, these records form a dependency graph across the toolchain. When an optimizer changes a parameter in a high-level C++ hardware model, every artifact derived from that parameter, such as generated RTL and its synthesized gate netlist, must be regenerated or shown to remain valid before reuse. A software testbench can be reused unchanged if its stimulus and reference checks do not depend on the altered behavior or interface, but it too must be rebuilt whenever the same parameter determines its expected outputs. Selective incremental rebuilding is safe only when the recorded dependencies capture every input that influences a transformation.

Dependency invalidation then walks this transformation history as a directed acyclic graph (@fig-artifact-lineage), allowing a later search iteration to branch off existing artifacts without overwriting the lineage of earlier evaluations.

![**Evaluated software and hardware artifacts retain explicit parent transformation lineage.** A single architectural intent branches into parallel software compilation and hardware elaboration paths. Each intermediate artifact (binary executable, Verilog RTL, gate netlist) inherits cryptographic parent hashes, tool versions, and operating conditions. Modifying any upstream input or configuration generates a distinct evaluation identity rather than overwriting existing records. The diagram is schematic; its hash labels are placeholders, not recorded digests.](images/fig-artifact-lineage.svg){#fig-artifact-lineage width="80%" fig-alt="Lineage diagram in which a single Lighthouse intent branches into a software variant and a hardware variant. The software compiles into an identified binary, and the hardware elaborates into an identified RTL artifact. An evaluation instance binds both artifacts to the tool and version, workload, and operating conditions. Hashes and evaluation keys distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

To identify the exact combination under test, the environment constructs an evaluation key from all declared inputs that distinguish one evaluation from another, including content hashes of the design artifacts and workload, tool and container versions, and relevant command settings. Upgrading a compiler version therefore produces a new evaluation key even if the output binary happens to be unchanged, whereas repeated executions of the same evaluation key still receive separate execution records so their individual outcomes and compute costs remain distinct.

Operating conditions belong in this history as well. In physical timing analysis, a slack of -12\ ps at a slow corner and a slack of -12\ ps at a typical corner describe different physical regimes; they can be compared only when those corner conditions stay attached to the metric rather than treated as interchangeable numbers. Software and simulator measurements are similarly sensitive to environmental details outside the source program: experiments have shown that changing nothing more than Unix link order or shell environment-variable layout can shift memory alignment enough to bias performance comparisons [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. The practical defense is to record every execution condition that can affect the property being measured.

Recording this lineage makes every run traceable and supplies the metadata needed to repeat it, though proving that a transformation preserved behavior or that a rerun will reproduce the result still requires verification checks, accessible artifacts, and a working execution procedure. While lineage records tell the harness which artifacts and checkpoints belong to a requested configuration, typed tool interfaces enforce those identities whenever a search method submits an action or reads back a result.

### Typed Tool Interfaces

When an optimizer or generative model drives EDA tools by assembling raw Tcl snippets or command-line strings, a picosecond-versus-nanosecond unit mismatch or a misspelled library path is often discovered only after the job waits in a cluster queue and checks out a commercial license seat, or worse, falls back to a default flag and silently evaluates the wrong corner. During setup, a typed environment contract prevents those string-level errors by defining the actions a search method can take and specifying each action's required inputs, permitted design changes, preconditions, and returned fields. Strong types make the structural requirements explicit by distinguishing a source-code handle, a clock period with units, and a wall-clock timeout even when a command-line tool eventually receives all three as text strings. Because type checking alone cannot verify that a cell library matches a design or that a requested analysis makes sense for an unmapped netlist, the contract pairs field types with domain preconditions.

For the coherence controller example, an environment might expose separate actions to submit an RTL implementation, synthesize an identified version, and evaluate its timing. A synthesis request identifies the source artifact, top-level module, target library, and clock constraints, while its return identifies any generated netlist and log reports alongside execution and parsing status. If the study holds the technology library fixed, the interface resolves that library from the study configuration and rejects requests that try to override it. An interface that accepts arbitrary module implementations lets a generator revise the controller anywhere within the study's scope, whereas one limited to predefined scalar parameters confines the search to the knob settings that parameter list anticipates.

Across the tool classes in @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum, interfaces can share a common envelope for request identifiers, job submission and cancellation, execution status, output references, compute cost, and error diagnostics. Inside that envelope, however, each tool class needs its own domain definitions. Synthesis with Yosys and physical layout with OpenROAD consume different design files and constraints [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD], and an adapter for a commercial tool must also declare its license features, file formats, and access restrictions. Keeping domain payloads distinct prevents a search method from treating a timing slack in picoseconds and an architectural simulator's instructions per cycle (IPC) estimate as interchangeable quantities merely because both return as numeric fields.

When an action modifies hardware structure rather than scalar parameters, a structured intermediate representation (IR) makes the allowed transformation easier to express and check than raw text substitution. Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) builds on Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) to provide hardware dialects whose `hw`, `comb`, and `seq` operations explicitly represent module boundaries, combinational logic, and sequential state elements [@CIRCT]. Exposing these IR structures through the tool interface guarantees that a proposed edit stays structurally well formed, though downstream simulation or formal checks are still required after the edit because structural validity does not prove that the revised circuit meets its functional specification.

Before a search loop relies on an interface implementation, small test fixtures should exercise it by pairing sample requests with expected tool inputs and representative tool logs with expected parsed returns, covering unit conversion, unsupported settings, and missing outputs alongside clean runs. Following the precedent of systematic fault-recovery testing in distributed systems such as FATE and DESTINI [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini], failure injection should also test hardware-tool failure modes (including timeouts, killed processes, and truncated log files) to verify that the wrapper returns the promised status and retains useful diagnostics. With individual actions and their failure behaviors verified, the next setup question is how to combine multiple tools to evaluate the properties the study needs.

### Multi-Tool Toolchains and Fidelity

A revised controller raises several questions: does it behave correctly, how does it affect workload execution, and can its implementation meet timing? Different tools address different parts of that evaluation. Whereas @sec-data-representations-world-models explained which design representations expose which hardware properties, here the environment binds those representations into executable tool paths, each with its own required inputs, simplifying assumptions, and outputs.

In this context, fidelity describes how faithfully a model represents a specific property under study rather than placing every tool on a single universal ranking. An RTL simulation exposes cycle-by-cycle protocol behavior that an analytical model omits, static timing analysis computes gate and wire delays that an unannotated RTL simulation ignores, and a formal check proves stated invariants under its declared assumptions. Greater detail in one of these evaluations cannot replace missing coverage in the others.

Because these complementary tool classes answer distinct questions rather than forming a single linear pipeline that every candidate must traverse (@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum), a study can stage its evaluations economically. The harness can run independent checks in parallel and use fast models to screen candidates before launching expensive evaluations, whenever the fast screen has been validated for the property and operating range in question.

How much of this multi-stage screening a study needs depends on how far the automated search can alter the hardware. When an optimizer tunes parameters inside a fixed structural template that has already been physically implemented, the study can sometimes rely mainly on a single tier, such as cycle-level simulation or an analytical wirelength proxy, so long as the search stays within the parameter region where that tier was calibrated. Once a generator or optimizer alters microarchitectural structure, that assurance disappears: an unconventional proposal can exploit blind spots in heuristic estimators, raising simulated IPC while producing an unroutable layout or failing power-integrity checks. An environment for structural search therefore arranges the tool classes of @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum into staged evaluation, where fast analytical and functional models reject broken candidates early, cycle-level simulators measure dynamic throughput on the survivors, and physical implementation and signoff tools check layout, timing, and power within the limits of their target libraries, corners, and assumptions.

| **Tool class** | **Representative use** | **What it models or checks** | **Preserved environment state** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical / circuit model | CACTI, spreadsheet models [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Analytical equations and technology assumptions without workload execution. | Model version, macro geometry, PVT conditions, technology limits. |
| Compiler and build stack | TVM, IREE, LLVM pass pipelines, linkers. | Generation of executable binaries; no hardware timing. | Source intermediate representations (IRs), target instruction set architecture (ISA) flags, compiler versions, binary hashes. |
| Functional ISA emulator | Spike, QEMU ISA execution. | Instruction semantics without microarchitectural timing. | Target binary, ISA extensions, input state, functional output. |
| Timing simulation | gem5 [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5], SST, Ramulator 2, SCALE-Sim. | Pipeline, cache, network-on-chip (NoC), memory controller, and accelerator timing. | Workload inputs, traces, warmup length, seeds, event traces. |
| RTL simulation / testbench | Verilator [@Veripool2026Verilator], cocotb, Synopsys VCS. | Cycle behavior under RTL semantics; no routed delay unless annotated. | RTL hash, testbench, compile flags, waveform traces. |
| Formal verification | SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) via SymbiYosys or JasperGold [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. | Stated invariants/relations under declared proof methods and bounds. | Property definitions, bounds, solver engine, proof certificates. |
| Emulation and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) | ZeBu, Palladium, FireSim on cloud FPGAs [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated target execution. FPGA mapping is not application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) signoff. | Target bitstream, host allocation, workload snapshot, traces. |
| Physical implementation and signoff | OpenROAD flow; OpenSTA timing; KLayout / Calibre DRC/LVS [@OpenROADDocs]. | Placement, routing, extracted parasitics, timing closure, and physical design-rule checks. | Netlist, library/PDK views, SDC constraints, layout and parasitic artifacts, operating corners, stage settings, rule decks. |
: **Fidelity is relative to the property under evaluation.** Harnesses preserve model assumptions, inputs, stages, and artifacts rather than collapsing returns into scalar scores. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

Even within a single row of @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum, what a returned result establishes depends on how the tool was run. A formal verification record must identify the checked property and environmental assumptions, and distinguish bounded model checking from an unbounded inductive proof such as $k$-induction.[^fn-k-induction-c06] Because a completed bounded check says nothing about failures that require more cycles than its bound, the harness must keep the proof bound attached to the result so downstream methods use it only within its scope.

[^fn-k-induction-c06]: **$k$-induction**: A formal proof method with two obligations. The base case establishes the property along executions from allowed initial states through the chosen depth. The inductive step establishes that, for any transition sequence admitted by the model, the property holding for $k$ consecutive states implies that it holds in the next state. Both obligations must succeed under the declared assumptions to establish the invariant beyond a bounded check.

Sampled simulation requires similar context in the returned record. Techniques such as SimPoint and SMARTS[^fn-simpoint-smarts-c06] let cycle-level simulators evaluate selected execution intervals to estimate full-workload behavior [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The environment must retain the interval-selection method, slice weights, warmup lengths, and checkpoint dependencies so downstream analysis knows which program phases were sampled and how their observations form the overall estimate.

[^fn-simpoint-smarts-c06]: **Simulation sampling**: SimPoint selects intervals based on program phases; SMARTS uses systematic sampling. Both reduce the amount of detailed execution that must be simulated. Their sampling and warmup assumptions remain part of the resulting performance estimate.


A unified design configuration connects these disparate evaluation paths across a project. In an SoC integration framework such as Chipyard [@chipyard], a single root configuration lowers through Chisel elaboration and FIRRTL transformations before fanning out into specialized evaluation backends (@fig-chipyard-framework). This shared origin lets software RTL simulation, physical VLSI implementation, and FPGA-accelerated execution start from the same microarchitectural parameters. Branch-specific settings and transformations must still be recorded independently; a shared top-level configuration guarantees common starting parameters, but it does not ensure that different backends evaluate identical physical or timing behavior.

![**Unified design configurations anchor multi-tool evaluation flows.** In this architectural flow based on the Chipyard SoC framework [@chipyard], a single root configuration lowers through Chisel generation and FIRRTL transformations before fanning out into specialized evaluation toolchains: software RTL simulation (Verilator/Synopsys VCS), very-large-scale integration (VLSI) physical design (Hammer with OpenROAD or commercial engines), and FPGA-accelerated simulation (FireSim). Shared configuration lineage preserves parameter traceability across fidelity tiers without conflating distinct physical returns. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-chipyard-framework.svg){#fig-chipyard-framework width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which a common design configuration lowers through Chisel generation and compiler transformations before branching into RTL simulation, VLSI physical implementation, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

Although shared configuration history traces a result back to its originating candidate, each output retains the semantic limits of its specific evaluation path: cycle counts from an unannotated Verilator testbench cannot substitute for post-route timing slack, FPGA execution rates are not ASIC clock frequencies, and FPGA resource utilization may reward a design that maps efficiently to lookup tables without establishing its standard-cell area. Using an upstream quantity as a proxy for a downstream property always requires empirical evidence for that relationship, which is why the environment keeps the tool identity, model assumptions, operating conditions, and units bound to every metric.

Evaluation throughput is equally tied to what each backend models. For example, ZSim reports about 20\ MIPS (million instructions per second) per simulated core, or roughly a $200\times$ slowdown for its detailed out-of-order model [@ZSim], whereas the FireSim paper reports a 1,024-node target cluster running on cloud FPGAs at a simulated processor clock rate of 3.4\ MHz, less than $1{,}000\times$ slower than its 3.2\ GHz target [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Because host instructions per second and simulated target cycles per second count different work against different reference systems, those figures describe distinct modeling regimes rather than a direct speed comparison.

@tbl-ch06-simulation-spectrum pairs each execution path with its reporting unit and the conditions that comparisons must match. Once a study selects a tool path that observes the required property, the harness can budget evaluation work in those path-specific units, separating one-time compilation or FPGA bitstream generation cost from the marginal cost of subsequent workload runs that reuse the built image.

| **Execution path** | **Unit of work or elapsed time** | **Conditions to match** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Analytical model | Model evaluations / second | Model, candidate size, host |
| ISA execution | Instructions / second | ISA, workload, host |
| Timing / RTL simulation | Target cycles / host second | Target model, workload, host |
| Hardware emulation | Target cycles / host second | Mapped target, workload, testbed |
| Formal verification | Elapsed time / named property | Property, model, bound, solver |
| Physical implementation | Elapsed time / defined stage | Design, libraries, stage settings |
: **Throughput comparisons require a declared unit of work.** Different execution paths count different work: model evaluations, instructions, target cycles, properties, or physical flow stages. The final column identifies conditions needed before even two rates in the same row can be compared. Row order implies no throughput or fidelity ranking. Author-constructed comparison guide, not a measured benchmark. {#tbl-ch06-simulation-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

Existing orchestration frameworks provide different parts of this multi-tool integration: ArchGym connects search algorithms to architecture simulators [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], CHIA supports hardware-software co-design workflows that combine design tools, simulators, software builds, and model calls [@CuiEtAl2026CHIA], and workflow engines such as Nextflow and Snakemake schedule execution dependencies [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow; @KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. Regardless of which framework a team builds upon, the study still has to specify which tool path answers each architectural question, which artifacts pass between stages, and what conditions permit reuse. Once those static tool paths, typed interfaces, and lineage rules are configured, the harness must manage their runtime execution as concurrent requests queue, run, and fail on shared cluster hardware.

## Running Parallel Tool Jobs Without Losing State

In an active search campaign, an optimizer regularly proposes a new candidate while an earlier multi-hour gem5 simulation or OpenROAD place-and-route job is still running on the cluster. Without runtime coordination, the new submission can overwrite RTL or constraint files in a live workspace, a batch-scheduler preemption can erase the accounting record of compute time and license hours already spent, and a stalled job can hold a commercial license seat indefinitely.

At runtime, the harness prevents those collisions by isolating each attempt's working directory, admitting requests only as compute slots and EDA licenses open up, tracking active runs across cluster nodes, and binding returned reports, exit statuses, and resource costs to the exact inputs and checkpoints that produced them. An asynchronous interface lets the optimizer submit a candidate and continue exploring while the harness tracks in-flight attempts, contains failures, and decides when completed artifacts can be reused. Supporting that loop starts with submitting and monitoring jobs without accidentally launching duplicate runs.

### Scheduling Parallel Runs and Making Retries Safe

In a synchronous interface, such as the `step()` call in reinforcement learning (RL) environments like Gymnasium [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium], the call blocks until the action finishes and returns its result directly. Blocking is convenient when an evaluation takes milliseconds, but hardware simulations and physical-design runs can take hours or days. Separating job submission from completion lets a search method submit a candidate, monitor outstanding requests, and continue other work while tools execute through a scheduler adapter connected to Slurm, IBM LSF, or a container service.

Once submission and completion are decoupled, the harness has to distinguish what was requested from how it executes on the cluster. A *request* describes the intended evaluation, an *attempt* records one effort to carry it out, and *backend jobs* perform the actual work across compute nodes. Because a single attempt can map to zero, one, or many backend jobs, the harness keeps its durable execution record separate from those transient cluster processes (@fig-runtime-object-state). A request refused at admission still leaves an execution record even though no cluster job ever starts. An admitted request, by contrast, may launch a single process or fan out across multiple parallel execution segments whose outputs, exit causes, and compute costs are reconciled into that single record. When a run fails and study policy permits a retry, the harness creates a new attempt linked explicitly to its predecessor.

![**A single execution record tracks zero, one, or multiple backend tool executions.** The execution record anchors all backend tool executions to the authorized request, whether the request is refused prior to execution, creates a single tool job, or spawns multiple parallel execution segments. The record preserves returned raw artifacts, realized compute and license costs, and independent status attributes including scheduling state, terminal cause, parser health, and retry parent links. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-runtime-object-state.svg){#fig-runtime-object-state width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual state diagram in which an authorized request creates one attempt. The attempt may be refused before a backend job exists, may create one job, or may create several jobs or execution segments. All paths feed one execution record. The execution record points separately to returned artifacts and realized cost. Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, cancellation confirmation, and retry parent remain independent attributes."}

Because an execution record must outlive the processes that perform its work, the harness retains available logs and records the resources already consumed whenever a cluster scheduler preempts a simulation. It tracks six status attributes independently: scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser health, cancellation confirmation, and retry parentage. Keeping these fields separate stops one status from masking another. When a scheduler evicts and requeues a job under the same attempt, each execution segment adds to that attempt's cumulative cost history; when the harness instead launches a fresh recovery attempt, it creates a new execution record linked to its predecessor. Neither path erases the interruption or the consumed core-hours.

Decoupled submission also introduces a classic distributed-systems hazard: the harness accepts a submission, but a network drop or timeout prevents its reply from reaching the caller. Resending that request must not launch a second copy of a multi-hour job. An *idempotent* submission produces the same system state when repeated [@Featonby2021IdempotentAPIs]. When a caller resubmits the same `submission_token` with the same request contents, the harness returns the existing attempt rather than creating another, and it rejects any call that reuses an old token with modified parameters. Retransmitting a submission whose outcome is unknown is therefore distinct from deliberately retrying failed work, which always uses a fresh token and creates a new, linked attempt.

Making submission genuinely idempotent requires more than checking a token in memory. The harness must record the accepted attempt in durable storage before dispatch and bind the token to the request and its backend jobs. If the harness crashes during dispatch, recovery has to check whether the cluster job already started before launching it again. While that check is underway, `poll` returns `RECONCILING` to indicate that the attempt is registered while its execution state remains uncertain. The caller can continue polling the existing attempt rather than submitting the same work under a new token that would create a duplicate, and recovery must resolve the uncertainty rather than assuming no job started.

The four operations in @lst-harness-interface expose this lifecycle cleanly. Calling `submit` returns an attempt identifier and admission status; `poll` reports progress; and `collect` retrieves the execution record once the attempt reaches a terminal state, including any partial outputs and failures. When several backend jobs belong to an attempt, the harness aggregates their individual states so that one completed job never marks the whole attempt complete prematurely. Finally, `cancel` requests termination, which must be confirmed across all attached work.

Beneath that caller-facing interface, the harness drives an explicit state machine for backend jobs (@fig-job-lifecycle). Cluster schedulers preempt long-running simulations and reclaim compute nodes, and the harness has to handle those intermediate transitions without corrupting the attempt they belong to.

![**Explicit scheduling states isolate cluster preemption from candidate evaluation.** A backend job transitions from queued through running to terminal completed, failed, or evicted states. Preempted runs requeue without losing prior execution segments, while retries generate linked attempts. Terminal states finalize compute and license accounting without conflating process termination with architectural validity. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-job-lifecycle.svg){#fig-job-lifecycle width="85%" fig-alt="State machine diagram in which an admitted job transitions from queued to running, branching into terminal completed or failed states, or an evicted state that cycles back to queued."}

Each state in that lifecycle records what happened to the process, not whether the hardware candidate is valid. A transition to `Completed` indicates only that the underlying operating-system process exited with code zero; it does not guarantee that the tool generated valid metrics or satisfied design constraints. In a static timing engine, a clean exit can occur even when unconstrained clock paths mask real violations or when false-path waivers suppress critical timing endpoints. Conversely, an `Evicted` state means the cluster scheduler preempted the job or reclaimed its node rather than that the candidate failed, so the harness requeues the work while linking the new execution segment to the earlier one. Exploration methods see only the attempt states that @lst-harness-interface returns, not the backend churn beneath them.

```{.yaml #lst-harness-interface lst-cap="**Harness interface shape.** Three normal-path calls submit, poll, and collect an attempt. Polling distinguishes unresolved execution state from known progress or completion. A fourth operation requests cancellation and reports whether termination is confirmed. Refused requests also retain an identifier and a collectable record."}
submit:
  takes: typed request, submission_token
  returns: attempt_id, admission status (ADMITTED | REFUSED)
poll:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: >-
    REFUSED | QUEUED | RUNNING | EVICTED | RECONCILING |
    COMPLETED | FAILED | CANCELED
collect:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: execution record (artifacts, parse status, cost, lineage)
cancel:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: CONFIRMED after all attached work stops | UNCONFIRMED (quarantine)
```

While idempotency prevents duplicate work, it does not limit the rate of distinct requests. As the capacity analysis in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization showed, a fast proposal method can easily overload a slower evaluation stage. The runtime harness enforces that capacity plan through admission limits, bounded queues, and backpressure signals that tell the caller to slow or pause submissions. Even then, free capacity at one stage does not guarantee capacity at the next, because available processors may still be waiting for tool licenses or upstream results.

Commercial EDA licenses introduce a second scheduling hazard beyond simple queue saturation. License managers grant checkouts per licensed feature, such as compilation, simulation runtime, or waveform viewing, rather than from a pool of interchangeable slots. Suppose an upstream job holds a compilation license while waiting for a simulation license, and the job holding that simulation license waits in turn for a compilation license. Both jobs now hold one resource while waiting for another in a cycle, meeting the conditions for deadlock [@CoffmanEtAl1971SystemDeadlocks]. Reserving every license a job will need before admitting it removes the hold-and-wait condition, while bounded queue depths keep the backlog within stage capacities. Neither measure, however, guarantees that a slow job will finish before concurrent changes move its input assumptions when tool runtimes are unpredictable (@sec-law-congestion-collapse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).

### Fault Containment and Execution Quarantines

Managing queues and licenses keeps work moving, but the harness also has to clean up safely when a run times out or fails midway. Suppose a synthesis job reaches its wall-clock limit and the harness requests cancellation. If the launcher script exits while a background worker it started is still writing a design database to disk, reusing that workspace for an immediate retry could mix files from the two attempts. Containing a fault requires tracking every process and writable resource belonging to an attempt and verifying whether any of them remain active before recycling the workspace.

On Linux, control groups (cgroups) track a job's local process tree as a unit: the cgroup v2 `cgroup.kill` interface terminates every process in the group and its descendants together, while the group's status file reports whether live processes remain.[^fn-process-containment-c06] Packaging commercial EDA flows into rootless OCI containers adds filesystem isolation, though enterprise tools impose practical constraints on containerization: license checkout can depend on host network access or on host identifiers such as a network-interface hardware address, shared high-throughput scratch filesystems require working POSIX file locking across network mounts, and multi-threaded signoff engines require tuned shared-memory (`/dev/shm`) allocations. Whatever local container or cgroup wrapper is used, terminating a local launcher never establishes that distributed workers on remote cluster nodes have exited; the harness must confirm termination through the cluster backend before reclaiming shared resources.

[^fn-process-containment-c06]: **Process containment**: Commercial EDA tools can spawn background daemons and child processes. If a parent script is killed, live orphaned workers may continue consuming memory and holding licenses. They differ from zombie processes, which have exited and await reaping. Linux `cgroups` (control groups) keep a job's processes in a tracked group so the harness can terminate them together and confirm exit before reclaiming resources.

When process termination cannot be confirmed, the harness places the affected execution in *quarantine*. Quarantine is an enforced operational lock rather than a passive status label: the harness seals the workspace, withholds partial outputs from publication, and marks uncertain resource and license allocations as unavailable for new work. A lingering worker may still write to the old directory, but it cannot reach a retry's workspace or corrupt shared candidate artifacts. When workspace isolation and the remaining study budget permit, a retry can proceed in a fresh directory under a separate resource allocation, while the quarantined attempt stays tracked until the harness confirms its processes have exited and can safely reclaim their resources.

Bounding how much work an attempt can consume requires separate enforcement controls for each resource class, including model calls, tool submissions, compute time, memory, scratch storage, and licenses. Capping process submissions does not bound a running tool's memory footprint, and killing a process does not prove that a commercial license seat is free. For commercial tokens, the harness must treat an allocation as busy until the license server's own release mechanism confirms that the checkout has been returned, rather than inferring release from a cancellation request.

When the harness retries a failed run, recovery has to preserve the study's accounting history. Retrying the same design under the same tool settings keeps its `candidate_id` and `configuration_id` while creating a new execution record linked to the failed attempt; if recovery modifies any input file or tool setting, those changes must receive a new configuration identifier. Each attempt retains its own outputs, measured resource use, and associated costs across compute time, memory and storage use, license occupancy, and any budgeted human repair effort. Whenever a crash or quarantine leaves a cost uncertain, the harness records that field as unknown rather than zero so that downstream methods never mistake an unfinished execution for a zero-cost evaluation.

### Categorizing Tool and Environment Failures

Keeping failed attempts distinct in the execution record also prevents a common modeling mistake: treating an infrastructure or tool failure as evidence that the candidate is a bad hardware design. A FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] license checkout denial means only that the tool could not acquire a seat; a host out-of-memory failure means the cluster node lacked enough memory to finish the run. Neither event establishes that the hardware is unroutable or fails timing. If the environment records either failure as a design defect, a surrogate predictor may learn false penalties and an optimizer may discard a promising candidate that never received its intended evaluation.

Choosing the right recovery action therefore begins by separating what happened during tool execution from what the returned files say about the hardware design. @tbl-failure-taxonomy lists nine execution conditions that the harness should keep distinct. Because a single run can trigger more than one condition (for example, a node preemption may leave behind a truncated report that also causes parsing to fail, while a completed timing run may report a setup violation), the harness records each status attribute independently and preserves earlier successful evaluations of the candidate when a later attempt fails.

| **Recorded condition** | **How it appears** | **Preserved evidence** | **Runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid request** | Illegal parameter or meaning-altering translation detected prior to invocation. | Request, validation rule, refusal reason. | Repair syntax only if meaning is preserved; otherwise refuse and return to caller. |
| **Setup / dependency failure** | Missing top-level, clock, library, constraint, or checkpoint. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, cost. | Restore or regenerate required inputs; record which evaluation could not proceed. |
| **Infrastructure failure** | License server unreachable, host out-of-memory (OOM), scheduler preemption. | Execution record, failure source, cost, retry eligibility. | Retry if policy and resources permit; retain any partial observations and mark the interrupted evaluation incomplete. |
| **Tool failure** | Crash or tool-reported execution error, such as a gem5 crash or failed elaboration. | Tool diagnostics, exit code, partial artifacts, cost. | Inspect the diagnostic to distinguish tool malfunction, input problems, and reported design errors before choosing recovery. |
| **Incomplete return** | Missing or truncated report files. | Stage records, produced files, raw logs, parse status. | Recover retained files or regenerate missing outputs where possible; rerun only the required work. |
| **Parser failure** | An available report cannot be interpreted according to the expected schema; absent source data may also indicate an incomplete return. | Parser version, raw log, recognized tokens, residual output. | Check the report and parser version; repair parsing and reparse if the required source data is present. |
| **Formal-tool return** | SVA/BMC tool returns a proof, counterexample, bounded result, or unresolved outcome. | Original status, method, property, model, assumptions, bound, available proof or counterexample trace, cost. | Preserve the exact status and its scope, including any timeout or other reason the check remains unresolved. |
| **Reported limit violation** | Completed run reports physical violation (OpenROAD worst negative slack (WNS) $< 0$, DRC error). | Typed violation, units, conditions, raw report, cost. | Record complete return without marking run as tool failure. |
| **Complete tool return** | Expected artifacts exist and parse cleanly (including limit violations). | Typed metrics, units, conditions, warnings, raw logs, cost, lineage. | Retain return for measurement qualification. |
: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.** Operational failures, partial returns, parser errors, and physical violations remain separate so recovery targets exact causes. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

Each of these conditions calls for a different next step. If a static timing tool finished cleanly but an updated report format broke the parser, fixing the parser and re-running it on the retained log recovers the result without launching another timing run. If a required cell library was missing at startup, the inputs must be repaired before the tool can answer the design question. And if a completed timing analysis reports negative slack, repeating the exact same run will only reproduce the violation; the design, constraints, or target assumptions need to change.

Formal verification returns demand the same care. A counterexample trace identifies a concrete violation of the stated property in the supplied model, whereas a solver timeout leaves the question unresolved. An unbounded proof holds only under its recorded environmental assumptions, and bounded model checking establishes the property only out to its step bound [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. The harness must store the formal tool's native status, assumptions, and bound alongside any normalized fields so that a shared schema never flattens a timeout or a bounded check into an unqualified pass.

Even a completed, cleanly parsed timing or physical report is meaningful only within the tool versions, libraries, operating corners, and constraint exceptions that governed the run. If an automated optimizer inserts a false-path exception[^fn-false-path-c06] simply to silence a timing violation, it has changed the check rather than fixed the hardware; similarly, a static timing analysis that omits dynamic IR drop[^fn-ir-drop-c06] cannot establish timing margin under heavy switching current. The environment must therefore retain those constraint files and analysis assumptions alongside the raw reports, warnings, and unrecognized log lines so that later review can catch what a parsed scalar summary left out.

[^fn-false-path-c06]: **False-path waivers**: Timing exceptions that exclude specified paths from static timing checks when functional behavior or clock relationships justify doing so. The exception must be supported by the declared design and clock assumptions; a path's absence from simulation is not sufficient. Asynchronous clock-domain crossings still require appropriate synchronization and clock-domain-crossing checks.

[^fn-ir-drop-c06]: **IR drop**: The voltage reduction (V = I $\times$ R) that occurs as current travels through the resistive metal layers of the power delivery network, which can cause transistors to switch slower or fail entirely under heavy toggle activity.


### Caching and Artifact Reuse

Automated hardware search faces a twin caching trap: rebuilding a compiled simulator binary or a multi-hour gate-level netlist from scratch for every downstream check wastes cluster compute and commercial license seats, yet reusing `netlist.v` simply because a file with that name sits on disk or passes a `Makefile` timestamp check can silently feed a netlist synthesized at a slow corner into a fast-corner power analysis. Recording exact inputs, tool versions, and operating conditions lets the harness avoid both errors by reusing completed work only when its upstream dependencies match the requested operation. Under that discipline, a compiled simulator binary can serve several candidates, a synthesized gate-level netlist can feed more than one downstream analysis, and a complete raw report can be reparsed after a parser repair without launching the tool again.

A cache key identifies the inputs and settings used to produce an artifact (including source contents, tool versions, PDK views, flags, workloads, and operating conditions), following the purely functional build discipline of identifying outputs through their complete dependency graph [@Dolstra2006Purely]. In a hardware flow, however, an omitted library corner or implicit tool default can still make two requests with matching keys evaluate different physical conditions. A cache key is therefore trustworthy only to the extent that its dependency list covers every input that shapes the output, and a matching file hash alone never proves that a cached library view or netlist fits the requested analysis.

Artifact reuse must also remain visible in the study's accounting. Returning a cached timing report supplies an existing observation rather than a fresh, independent measurement, so the new execution record must point to the original producing attempt and log the near-zero lookup cost separately from the compute hours spent generating the artifact. The same rule applies to generative steps: retained model context is a tracked input too, and reusing cached prompts or retrieved design context must follow the study's data-access and disclosure rules so that proprietary design context never silently enters an open-source baseline run.

Reusing a completed output file is simpler than resuming execution from an intermediate checkpoint or resetting a persistent tool session. Resuming from a checkpoint continues execution from saved state, which requires the harness to verify the checkpoint's inputs, tool configuration, and execution history before building on it. A *reset*, by contrast, restores the clean starting state required by the next attempt by initializing a fresh workspace or restoring a verified baseline checkpoint so that tool databases, emulator memory, and peripheral registers hold no leftover state. A fast soft reset that leaves memory buffers or peripheral registers populated is acceptable only when the study explicitly permits that retained state and records it.

Simply stopping a process does not reset an environment, nor does a matching checkpoint hash prove that state restoration succeeded. Reclaiming a commercial license seat is likewise a separate resource-management handshake governed by the license server rather than by workspace cleanup. Whenever work runs again, its execution record states whether it started from a cold workspace or continued from retained state, preserving the resource cost of each segment without counting the same work twice. The failure mode below shows why checking file identity without checking operating suitability breaks even a simple cache lookup.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The stale library view"}
**The trap.** In this illustrative failure, a design update reruns static timing analysis and receives a clean report indicating that the checked bus paths meet the requested clock period.

**The mechanism.** The analyzer loaded a cached library view that did not match the intended operating conditions. The report described checks under that stale view; it did not establish timing at the requested conditions.

**The lesson.** Before reusing a library view, the harness must check that it is the view required for the requested design and operating conditions. Checksums help identify PDK, LEF, and Liberty files, but compatibility also depends on their contents and intended use. A clean report from the wrong view cannot establish that the design meets timing under the intended conditions.
:::

### Separating Hardware Changes from Tool and Seed Noise {#sec-incremental-churn-dispersion}

Cache keys catch stale library views when inputs change within a run, but an evaluation can also go stale because the surrounding project moved on while a search was running. During an exploration campaign against a fixed baseline snapshot $t_0$, concurrent engineering work may update compiler passes, runtime software, tool versions, or RTL bus interfaces on the main branch. A candidate evaluated against snapshot $t_0$ may therefore need adaptation and re-evaluation before its results apply at $t_0 + \Delta t$. The earlier execution record still describes the original configuration accurately, but its numbers do not automatically carry over to the updated baseline.

Deciding how much work must be repeated after an upstream change is a practical bottleneck. Regenerating an entire accelerator and repeating physical synthesis after every small register or arbiter edit would make iterative search too slow for daily engineering work.
