To narrow what must be rerun, a harness can combine structural representations (such as CIRCT dialects, Chisel module hierarchies, and dependency-graph build tools like Bazel) to identify which downstream artifacts depend on the modified sources. Syntactic module boundaries, however, tell only part of the story: an unchanged file or module boundary does not by itself prove that a cycle-level simulation result or a formal verification conclusion still holds once neighboring blocks change.

Physical implementation makes that cross-module coupling concrete. In flattened placement and routing, a local register change inside one block can shift cell congestion, clock-tree structure, and wire routing across neighboring modules. Hierarchical floorplan partitioning can contain the work that must be repeated, provided the partition's interface, timing budgets, and physical assumptions continue to hold. The harness therefore records the basis for any artifact reuse alongside the stages repeated when upstream changes invalidate earlier assumptions, and it tracks divergence between an active search snapshot and the mainline so the study can pause, resynchronize, or rerun affected work under a declared policy.

Shifts across design revisions are distinct from variation across repeated executions of the exact same configuration. To keep run-to-run variation interpretable, the environment must separate three mechanisms:

- **Host runtime jitter.** CPU frequency scaling, NUMA migration, memory contention, and shared-storage load can alter wall-clock runtime and simulator throughput without changing the simulated guest cycle count of a deterministic run. Execution records preserve the host node placement, CPU governor, storage path, and other declared runtime conditions.
- **Explicit algorithmic randomness.** Generative models, stochastic search passes, and randomized EDA stages can produce different candidates, cell layouts, or timing metrics across runs. Records preserve random seeds wherever the tool exposes them, along with sampling and algorithm settings, and explicitly note when randomness controls are unavailable.
- **Parallel execution nondeterminism.** Multi-threaded tools can return different artifacts or metrics when thread counts or operating-system thread schedules change. Records preserve thread and concurrency settings rather than assuming that pinning a seed removes parallel nondeterminism.

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

Tool settings that the architectural hypothesis never mentions can shift returned metrics by amounts comparable to the hardware differences a study hopes to detect. In one retained dataset of 125 Yosys and ABC logic-synthesis runs targeting the Nangate 45\ nm library, five open designs were each mapped under 25 different ABC pass sequences while holding their RTL unchanged (@fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion). Across those 25 sequences, the spread of mapped cell area ranged from 3.5% of the median on an OpenPiton NoC router to about 15% (from 5% below to 10% above the median) on the `gcd` block, which computes a greatest common divisor. Because every run used a different pass sequence, these spreads measure sensitivity to the synthesis recipe rather than run-to-run variation at a fixed recipe; although the original harness was not retained, a reconstructed flow run on pinned public sources re-derives every recorded area exactly.

Explicit randomness inside a single fixed recipe leaves its own signature. In a separate pilot with pinned input sources and retained logs, twenty OpenROAD global-placement runs of the `gcd` example design from OpenROAD-flow-scripts on Nangate45 started from the same floorplan hash and differed only in the placement seed (the released records include intermediate database hashes without the binary floorplan or placement databases themselves). Across that single small design, flow stage, and host, detailed-placement area spanned 0.84% of its median and estimated setup WNS spanned 3.8% of its median magnitude. Together, the recipe and seed measurements drive home the same practical point: an optimizer that keeps only favorable outcomes without recording synthesis recipes and random seeds leaves downstream analysis unable to separate a genuine architectural improvement from a fortunate tool setting or seed.[^fn-lucky-seed-c06]

[^fn-lucky-seed-c06]: **Seed and recipe sensitivity**: Randomized stages such as stochastic placement, and heuristic settings such as logic-optimization pass order, give a distribution of outcomes rather than a single value. An improvement no larger than the spread across seeds or recipes cannot be attributed to a new method or design without evaluating several seeds or recipes and reporting the spread.

![**Unchanged RTL can return a different mapped area under a different synthesis recipe.** Each point is one of 25 ABC pass sequences applied to one of five open designs with Yosys on the Nangate 45\ nm library, 125 runs in all, plotted relative to each design's median area. The widest spread is on GCD. The runs vary the recipe rather than a random seed, and every plotted area is re-derived by a reconstructed flow on pinned sources.](images/fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion.png){#fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion width="100%" fig-alt="Box plot with overlaid points of 125 logic synthesis runs across five open hardware designs, showing mapped area as a percentage deviation from each design median. Spreads are 3.5 to 7.6 percent for the PicoRV32 core, NoC router, AES-128, and SHA-256 designs and about 15 percent for the GCD block, and each design is drawn with its own marker shape."}

These distributions show why an automated design loop cannot treat a single tool run as point truth. Heuristic logic-optimization passes such as rewriting, refactoring, and balancing are applied in sequence, so changing their order steers the optimization into different local minima with different area, runtime, and memory footprints. A credible study therefore has to budget for repeated evaluations, record exact recipes, seeds, and settings, and log resource consumption alongside quality-of-results metrics. @sec-feedback-verification-trust explains how downstream statistical methods test whether an observed gain reflects a genuine architectural improvement or tool variation; the environment's responsibility is to capture the complete execution records that make that test possible.

## Execution Records {#sec-execution-records}

When a harness returns only a bare dictionary of scalar metrics to the search loop, operational failures masquerade as hardware properties: an unparsed power report defaults to `0.0`, an in-place retry overwrites the license-hours burned by earlier crashes, and a single setup-slack number hides hold-time violations or unmeasured operating corners. Capturing the full context around those numbers is the job of the execution record, which brings together the information needed to answer three questions: what work was attempted, what happened at runtime, and what can be examined afterward? @sec-architecture-20-ontology defines the execution record as the core artifact connecting requested work to the state actually evaluated; at runtime, that definition becomes an explicit schema covering every attempt across the execution lifecycle. A refused request logs why no tool ran, an attempt spanning several backend jobs links their outcomes together, and a later retry adds to the candidate's history rather than overwriting the failed attempt.

Six groups of information make the record complete:

- **Request and attempt identity**: Study, request, run specification, candidate, configuration, workload, attempt universally unique identifier (UUID), submission token, and attached scheduler job identifiers.
- **Starting state**: Input artifacts, source revisions, tool and container versions, library views, and operating conditions.
- **Execution outcome**: Admission status, job outcomes, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and recovery eligibility.
- **Returned material**: Raw reports and logs, artifact references and hashes, structured metrics with units and scope, warnings, and unrecognized output.
- **Lineage and retries**: Dependencies, producing transformations, and links to earlier attempts or restored checkpoints, with references to any checks performed.
- **Resource use and cost**: Wall-clock time, CPU/accelerator hours, peak memory, storage use, license-hours, and charges, distinguishing measured values from estimates or unknowns.

Whenever an expected measurement or artifact is unavailable, the record states that absence and its cause explicitly so downstream analysis can distinguish a metric that was not measured from one that failed to parse or did not apply. Joining inputs, execution status, signoff metrics, and resource costs in the same schema also keeps complementary physical checks attached to one another. In static timing analysis, for example, evaluating timing health requires pairing worst negative slack (WNS, identifying the single most critical path) with total negative slack (TNS, integrating the delay deficit across all failing endpoints), failing endpoint counts, and hold slack across multi-mode multi-corner (MCMM) views. Retaining explicit references to raw reports, switching-activity profiles, power scopes, and execution costs (wall-clock time, memory footprint, and tool license-hours) lets independent reviewers verify which operating corners produced each metric and weigh hardware performance against the full cost of exploration.

The depth of record a study needs grows with how much of the design the automated loop may change. Manually driven drafting often relies on informal records such as developer notes, terminal logs, and version-control commits, while a harness running parameter sweeps can automate tracking of parameter vectors, simulator seeds, and scalar cost metrics. Once a system changes structure across abstraction boundaries, however, its records must preserve the full chain linking high-level intent, intermediate compiler representations, synthesized netlists, place-and-route databases, and signoff reports. Even then, the record documents which checks ran and what they returned; it does not by itself certify that a design is physically viable.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import csv as _csv6sc
import json as _json6sc
from pathlib import Path as _Path6sc
import _python.plots as _ap6sc

_sc20_dir = _Path6sc(_ap6sc.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "20-implementation-stage-costs"
_sc20_bounds = _json6sc.loads((_sc20_dir / "time_boundaries.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_sc20_rows = list(_csv6sc.DictReader((_sc20_dir / "stage-costs.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
_sc20_top = max(_sc20_rows, key=lambda r: float(r["runtime_seconds"]))
```

Complete records also support later efforts to reproduce the work. The ACM artifact review guidelines distinguish *repeatability* (same team, same setup), *reproducibility* (different team, same setup), and *replicability* (different team, different setup) [@ACM2020ArtifactReview], and the Popper convention similarly emphasizes preserving executable evaluation workflows [@JimenezEtAl2017PopperConvention]. An execution record supplies the metadata needed for these activities, though carrying them out still requires access to the underlying artifacts and a runnable procedure. Even with identical recorded inputs, host runtime or returned metrics can vary for the reasons examined in @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion, and wall-clock cost itself shifts depending on whether the record measures individual tool steps or the enclosing job (@fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs).

![**Recorded runtime depends on which execution boundary the harness measures.** (a) Longest individual step intervals and combined remainder across all `{python} sc20_steps_n` outer steps (`{python} sc20_sum_s`\ s total) in a retained LibreLane physical-implementation run of the `spm` test design on the open IHP SG13G2 130\ nm BiCMOS PDK [@LibreLane2026SpmSg13g2Run; @IHPOpenPDK]. Detailed routing in OpenROAD is the single longest step (`{python} sc20_route_s`\ s). (b) Nested accounting boundaries for the same run: summed step intervals (`{python} sc20_sum_s`\ s), the enclosing `Run Test` workflow action (`{python} sc20_test_s`\ s), and the complete continuous-integration job including environment setup (`{python} sc20_job_s`\ s).](images/fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs){#fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel horizontal bar chart of recorded execution times from a single LibreLane physical-implementation run on the IHP SG13G2 PDK. Panel (a) shows the six longest individual tool steps led by OpenROAD detailed routing at 25.76 seconds alongside the combined remainder of the 78 steps totaling 106.3 seconds. Panel (b) compares three nested accounting boundaries: the 106.3-second sum of step intervals, the 108.0-second Run Test action, and the 288.0-second complete CI job."}

In that retained LibreLane run on the IHP SG13G2 PDK [@LibreLane2026SpmSg13g2Run], the `{python} sc20_steps_n` recorded tool steps sum to `{python} sc20_sum_s`\ s (led by OpenROAD detailed routing at `{python} sc20_route_s`\ s, followed by Magic LEF generation, streamout, and design-rule checks), whereas the enclosing `Run Test` action spans `{python} sc20_test_s`\ s and the complete continuous-integration job spans `{python} sc20_job_s`\ s (`{python} sc20_job_over_steps` times the summed step intervals once container and environment setup are included). Because those three intervals nest rather than add, a study that compares tool runtimes across runs must state which accounting boundary its execution record reports. Just as a runtime figure is interpretable only alongside its accounting boundary, artifact lineage shows how files were produced while references to behavioral checks show what was actually tested rather than what content hashes alone prove. Stepping through our prospective mobile XR study shows how these environment rules and execution records fit together in practice.

## Mobile XR Subsystem Evaluation Environment {#sec-mobile-xr-evaluation}

The prospective Lighthouse cache study provides a compact example of how an environment turns a study plan into conditional tool execution. It compares 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB cache capacities while holding the surrounding compute organization, software stack, and workload fixed. As introduced in @sec-moonshot, the illustrative subsystem pairs an NPU ($16 \times 16$ array) and dual LPDDR5X channels under a 3\ W power budget in a 3\ nm-class process such as TSMC N3E. These choices describe one prospective study plan rather than a completed Lighthouse implementation.

To run that plan, the environment must translate candidate requests into tool invocations and handle their returns and failures according to @tbl-environment-contract. The study is not yet executable because the capacity-to-hardware construction rule, controlled parameters, tool inputs, and measurement procedures still need to be bound; while those prerequisites remain incomplete, the lifecycle requires stopping before cluster dispatch (@sec-architecture-20-ontology). The walkthrough below runs the analytical screen with a real SRAM model and then traces a hypothetical sequence to illustrate the cycle-level execution that follows. It also adds an illustrative analytical screening rule to the study card of @sec-architecture-20-ontology, whose four-execution budget allots one cycle-level trial per capacity plus one rerun; under that rule, a candidate that fails analytical screening leaves its cycle-level trial available to the rest of the budget.

| **Run category** | **Prospective XR subsystem evaluation plan** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | Vary only `l2.capacity` among 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB. Hold the NPU organization, RISC-V cores, memory arbitration, NoC, software binary, XR workload, and cache policies fixed. A specified rule must derive each legal SRAM organization from capacity; capacity alone does not identify its banks, geometry, or macro composition. |
| **Translation and identity** | Prepare analytical SRAM-model inputs and a compatible cycle-level simulation path, such as configured gem5 and Ramulator 2 models. Identify relevant process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions, libraries, wrappers, parsers, tool versions, and seeds. Any Verilator or SCALE-Sim path needs its own representations and supported scope. Power estimates require an identified model or engine, activity inputs, and applicable UPF power intent. |
| **Order and dispatch** | Once prerequisites are bound, perform analytical screening. Admit cycle-level work only when the screening return is complete, matches its schema, and reports area $\le 1.5\text{ mm}^2$ and access time $\le 2.5\text{ ns}$. Passing this screening check permits further evaluation; it does not establish candidate superiority. |
| **Matched work and limits** | Use matched workload and operating conditions for baseline and alternatives. Budget three screening runs and at most four cycle-level attempts, including recovery attempts. Apply specified queue, execution, and study deadlines. RTL synthesis and physical signoff are outside this exploratory budget. |
| **Failures and recovery** | Keep infrastructure failures, tool errors, incomplete returns, and parser failures distinct. Reparse retained material when sufficient; when execution must be retried, create a linked attempt from the required starting state and charge it to the budget. |
| **Containment and reuse** | Restrict each attempt's access to tools and writable paths. Quarantine unconfirmed terminations. Reuse artifacts only when their dependencies and conditions match the intended operation, preserving links to the producing attempts. |
| **Returns, cost, and lineage** | Retain SRAM area, access time, energy and leakage estimates; frame records, memory traffic, and subsystem power with their model and activity assumptions. NPU area and multiply-accumulate (MAC) utilization belong with the relevant NPU model if that path is used. Preserve raw reports, warnings, inputs, outputs, costs, and dependency links. |
| **Decisions left outside** | The harness enforces the supplied dispatch and stopping rules. The method or architect determines measurement validity, comparative conclusions, and whether to advance a candidate or revise the study. |
: **An environment executes the study's rules while retaining their inputs and consequences.** This prospective plan separates preparation, conditional dispatch, recovery, and interpretation; it is not a completed execution specification. {#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Screening returns for the three Lighthouse capacities: CACTI 7 output written by
# data/run_cacti_lighthouse_l2.py from data/cacti_lighthouse_l2.cfg.in.
_cacti_csv = (
    _root / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "06-environments" / "data"
    / "cacti-lighthouse-l2.csv"
)
with open(_cacti_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _cacti = {
        (r["device_type"], int(r["capacity_mib"])): r
        for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))
    }
assert len(_cacti) == 6


def _cv(device, mib, col):
    return float(_cacti[(device, mib)][col])


_mibs = (2, 3, 4)
hp_area = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'area_mm2'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
hp_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
lp_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-lstp', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
hp_leak_w = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'leakage_mw') / 1000:.2f}" for m in (2, 4)]
lp_leak_mw = [f"{_cv('itrs-lstp', m, 'leakage_mw'):.1f}" for m in (2, 4)]
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "access_time_ns") <= 2.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "access_time_ns") > 2.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "access_time_ns") > 2 * _cv("itrs-hp", m, "access_time_ns") for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "leakage_mw") > 1000 * _cv("itrs-lstp", m, "leakage_mw") for m in _mibs)
```

Running CACTI 7 [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI], the analytical SRAM model listed in @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum, on the Lighthouse cache candidates shows why a wrapper must refuse an unsupported technology node rather than silently substituting the closest available one. The pinned CACTI 7 version used here supports characterized nodes only down to 22\ nm rather than the 3\ nm-class Lighthouse target, so the wrapper cannot evaluate the requested node directly. If we run the 2, 3, and 4\ MiB candidates at 22\ nm anyway (with 64-byte lines, 16 ways, one bank, and internal array organizations chosen by CACTI's energy-delay-squared objective), high-performance devices return areas of `{python} hp_area[0]`, `{python} hp_area[1]`, and `{python} hp_area[2]`\ mm², access times of `{python} hp_acc[0]`, `{python} hp_acc[1]`, and `{python} hp_acc[2]`\ ns, and standby leakage of `{python} hp_leak_w[0]` to `{python} hp_leak_w[1]`\ W. Switching to low-standby-power devices under the same cache specifications shifts access times to `{python} lp_acc[0]` to `{python} lp_acc[2]`\ ns and drops leakage to `{python} lp_leak_mw[0]` to `{python} lp_leak_mw[1]`\ mW. Every 22\ nm area exceeds the $1.5\text{ mm}^2$ target limit, every high-performance access time passes the 2.5\ ns limit, and every low-standby-power access time fails it, yet none of those numbers answers the 3\ nm design question. The area and latency thresholds were written for a 3\ nm-class macro, and the unbound choice of device family alone moves access time by more than a factor of two and leakage by more than three orders of magnitude. Under the wrapper translation rule established earlier, the wrapper reports the node mismatch as a limitation rather than emitting a false screening verdict, and cycle-level admission waits for a model characterized at the target node (the configuration, script, and parsed returns are retained with the chapter data).

Suppose such a 3\ nm model were available and admitted the 2\ MiB and 3\ MiB candidates while rejecting the 4\ MiB candidate above an area or latency limit. Under this plan, the 4\ MiB candidate would receive no cycle-level dispatch; its screening record would remain on file for review, though failing an analytical screen would not by itself prove physical infeasibility.

A hypothetical execution sequence might then spend the four-attempt cycle-level budget as follows:

1. The 2\ MiB baseline completes a cycle-level evaluation.
2. The 3\ MiB attempt encounters a setup failure and returns no usable cycle-level result.
3. After the setup problem is repaired, a linked retry of the same 3\ MiB candidate completes under the intended conditions.
4. A planned repeat of the 3\ MiB evaluation consumes the final attempt.

Inspecting the execution records afterward shows four attempts on the books, but only three completed cycle-level evaluations. The failed attempt preserves its setup diagnostics and consumed cost, and the recovery retry remains distinct from the planned repeat. This four-step trace illustrates honest accounting rather than a sufficient statistical comparison; the search method or architect still has to judge whether three completed runs support a design decision. What the environment provides is an auditable record of what was admitted, what ran, what returned, and what remained unresolved. How to test whether a clean return actually qualifies a candidate is the subject of @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

## Open Questions

Building isolated tool harnesses and keeping complete execution records exposes four open problems in how we run and audit hardware design tools:

- **How can we verify which checks a closed-source EDA tool actually ran without repeating the entire analysis?** A commercial synthesis or static timing engine can exit with code zero and print a cleanly formatted report while silently ignoring a requested operating corner, falling back to a default wire-load model, or skipping paths hidden by an inherited constraint waiver. Parsing text logs catches only the omissions a vendor binary chooses to print, yet rerunning the full analysis in a second reference tool gives up the speed the harness was built to provide. We still lack lightweight canary checks, input-perturbation probes, or execution-trace attestations that can confirm an opaque tool exercised the requested corners and constraints, keeping the runtime question of whether the requested check ran separate from the modeling question of whether that check adequately captures physical effects such as voltage droop.[^fn-voltage-droop-c06]

[^fn-voltage-droop-c06]: **Voltage droop**: A temporary decrease in supply voltage, which can occur when switching activity changes the current drawn from the power delivery network. It can change cell delays; assessing its timing consequences requires voltage assumptions or analyses that cover the relevant variation.

- **When we reuse a running hardware emulator or persistent EDA session across candidates, how do we guarantee that no state leaks from one run to the next?** Reinitializing an FPGA emulation cluster from a cold bitstream reload or rebuilding an in-memory physical-design database from scratch for every candidate can take longer than the evaluation itself. Warm resets and checkpoint continuations avoid that setup penalty, but they risk leaving residual state in external DRAM buffers, unmapped peripheral registers, or cached parasitic timing graphs that silently contaminates the next candidate's measurement. Early snapshot-and-restore harnesses in operating-system fuzzing hit the same problem, producing irreproducible crashes until copy-on-write memory isolation eliminated cross-test state pollution. We still need copy-on-write hardware state snapshots and reset-verification checks that can guarantee a warm emulator or tool session matches a cold start at a fraction of full reinitialization cost.

- **When an engineer or generator edits one hardware module, how do we know which cached layout and timing results elsewhere on the chip remain valid?** Content-addressed build systems track syntactic file dependencies cleanly, but physical chip implementation couples neighboring modules together. In flattened placement and routing, modifying a single arbiter or register stage can shift macro congestion, wire parasitics, and clock-tree skew across adjacent blocks whose source RTL never changed. Rerunning full-chip synthesis and place-and-route after every minor upstream edit makes continuous co-design too slow for daily work, whereas trusting module-level file hashes alone lets stale timing and power numbers slip through. We still lack reliable ways to combine intermediate compiler representations (such as CIRCT) with physical floorplan partitions and interface slack margins to prove when a local change stays contained within a region, triggering selective incremental re-evaluation only where physical coupling invalidates earlier execution records.

- **How can we tell a genuine architectural improvement from a lucky synthesis recipe or placement seed without multiplying our compute and license budgets?** As the synthesis and placement dispersion measurements in @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion demonstrate, varying logic-optimization pass orders or placement seeds on unchanged RTL can shift mapped area and timing slack by margins larger than the architectural effect under study. Running a full matrix of recipes and random seeds for every proposed candidate would quickly exhaust cluster compute and commercial EDA license seats, whereas evaluating a single seed invites an optimizer to mistake a fortunate tool run for a better microarchitecture. We still need adaptive scheduling policies that spend multi-seed and multi-recipe runs only on candidates whose estimated improvement sits inside the tool's noise band, while avoiding hold-and-wait license deadlocks across concurrent multi-tool pipelines.

## Summary

An execution environment connects design methods to the simulators, compilers, formal engines, and physical-design flows that construct and evaluate hardware candidates. During setup, the environment defines the actions a method may request (including whether it can submit new RTL or only adjust parameters inside a fixed template) and establishes the tool paths and lineage rules that identify every input. At runtime, the harness schedules work across cluster nodes and license pools, isolates faults, and records the history of each attempt so that returned observations carry enough context to show what each result actually describes.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Interfaces define the available design actions.** Specify what a method may inspect, submit, change, and evaluate. Wrappers translate those requests into tool inputs and return structured results without silently changing the candidate or its conditions.
- **Tool choice follows the property being evaluated.** Behavioral checks, timing models, formal analyses, and physical implementation answer different questions. Preserve each path's assumptions, scope, and units when combining their outputs, and expect staged evaluation to reach physical and formal checks once automated work may change structure.
- **Every execution attempt needs its own record.** Link requests to backend jobs, outputs, failures, and costs. Distinguish duplicate submissions from deliberate retries, enforce admission limits so proposals do not overwhelm evaluation capacity, and keep raw reports, warnings, and missing values beside the parsed metrics.
- **Recovery and reuse require controlled state.** Isolate writable workspaces, respect data-access restrictions, confirm termination, and manage shared licenses. Reuse an artifact or checkpoint only when it applies to the requested operation; a matching identifier alone is insufficient.
- **Repeated execution is part of the evaluation plan.** Budget for variation, retain recipes, seeds, and settings, and distinguish randomness from host interference and parallel nondeterminism. A cached result is an existing observation, not a new repeat.
:::

Recording what ran and what returned is the foundation for closing the design loop, but an execution record does not interpret itself. The next step is to decide what those observations actually prove and how they should steer the search. @sec-feedback-verification-trust connects verification, statistical feedback, and learning to that decision.
